articles.headline: THE LATEST. From Bismarck.--The Prosecution have rested. Sensational scene in Court.--Attorney Long to the Fore.
articles.text:
Bismarck, Dakota, Special To the Cow Boy, Sept. 17.

The prosecution rested yesterday, having only proved what is already known, that Luffsey was killed by the party, of which DeMores was a member.

This morning, witnesses McClung, Harmon and Walker testified that they heard Luffsey and O'Donald say the day before the shooting that they would shoot DeMores on sight. To-day's testimony is to the effect that they bore bad reputations, especially O'Donald.

A sensational scene was enacted in court this morning. Judge Francis and Prosecuting attorney T. K. Long became engaged in an unseemly wrangle, which ended in Long giving the Judge the lie direct. The Judge immediately committed Long to jail for contempt of court, where he now languishes. J. H.
articles.summary: Special dispatch from Bismarck reporting that the prosecution rested in the de Morès murder trial, defense witnesses testified to threats by Luffsey and O'Donald, and Judge Francis jailed prosecutor T. K. Long for contempt.

articles.text: The Sioux Falls constitutional convention is working away as hard as if their labor stood some chance of being recognized by Congress. They have about decided that the name of the new state shall be "Dacotah" with a "c" and a "haich," that the motto shall be "Under God the people rule" and that attendance at school shall be compulsory between the ages of six and twelve.
articles.summary: Skeptical note on the Sioux Falls constitutional convention's choice of the name "Dacotah," its motto and compulsory schooling.

articles.text: Bismarck is reaping a harvest in the case of the Territory vs. Marquis de Mores, E. G. Paddock et al. Everyone who knew anything of the case and about as many who knew nothing about it, have been subpœnæd as witnesses. They were also subpœnæd at least four days before they could by any possibility be needed. This gave all the witnesses time to go decently broke before their attention should be distracted by the trial, a state in which they were almost unanimously found last Saturday. If the Bismarck gang havn't the art of "blowing a man in," down fine, then indeed is it a lost art.
articles.summary: Sarcastic editorial on Bismarck profiting from the many witnesses subpoenaed early in the de Morès-Paddock case.

articles.text: The question of county organization has been discussed on a plain business basis and it is the opinion of all with whom we have conversed, that taking into consideration the recent assessment, it would cost less than to remain unorganized, provided an honest board of county commissioners is appointed. That these will be honest men, there can scarcely be a doubt, as the large majority of citizens now in the county are and will be in favor of honest men for commissioners, plenty of whom can be found here. The new law respecting the organization of counties, passed at the last session of the legislature, gives the governor no option in the matter and completely does away with his appointing a non-resident for a commissioner. The law was passed at the request of the present governor and compels him to organize a county and to appoint as commissioners the three men recommended in a petition signed by one hundred and fifty qualified voters; residents of the county. This law gives us an opportunity of recommending good men as commissioners. There are many such in the county, possessing the entire confidence of their fellow-citizens. This matter of organization must be attended to immediately, as the Territorial board of equalization has met and apportioned the tax. Meantime, we advise that any taxes paid to Stark county be paid under protest and they can then be reclaimed, either by Billings county or the individual tax-payers, as there is but little doubt as to the unconstitutionality of the law.
articles.summary: Editorial urging immediate organization of Billings County under the new territorial law, and advising that taxes paid to Stark County be paid under protest.

articles.text:
There being a very hazy impression abroad as to the definitions and degrees of homicide as defined by Dakota's Penal code, we publish the following from the charge of Judge Francis to the jury in the Magill case: "Homicide is the killing of one human being by another. Homicide is either:
1. Murder.
2. Manslaughter.
3. Excusable homicide, or
4. Justifiable homicide.
Homicide is murder in the following cases:
1. When perpetrated without authority of law and with a premeditated design to effect the death of the person killed or of any other human being.
2. When perpetrated by any act imminently dangerous to others and evincing a depraved mind regardless of human life, although without any premeditated design to effect the death of any particular individual.
3. When perpetrated without any design to effect death by a person engaged in the commission of any felony.
Homicide is manslaughter in the first degree in the following cases, viz:
1. When perpetrated without a design to effect death, by a person while engaged in the commission of a misdemeanor.
2. When perpetrated without a design to effect death, and in a heat of passion, but in a cruel and unusual manner, or by means of a dangerous weapon, unless it is committed under such circumstances as constitute excusable or justifiable homicide.
3. When perpetrated unnecessarily, either while resisting an attempt by the person killed to commit a crime, or after such attempt shall have failed.
Every killing of one human being by the act, procurement, or culpable negligence of another, which under the provisions of this chapter (which I have read to you) is not murder, nor manslaughter in the first degree, nor excusable nor justifiable homicide, is manslaughter in the second degree."

The verdict in this, the Magill case, was "Manslaughter in the second degree." The greatest punishment under this verdict is four years in the penitentiary. The defendant can be let off with a fine however. Sentence will be pronounced in a day or two.
articles.summary: Judge Francis's jury charge defining degrees of homicide in the Magill case, with the verdict of manslaughter in the second degree.

articles.text: In looking over the daily market reports one must often be puzzled to understand why it is that side by side he will find scales of stock of similar or identical average weights showing a difference in price of fifty cents, seventy-five cents, and $1.00 per hundred, as the case may be. A farmer will also marvel that the car-load of big, fat, but rough cattle which he had flattered himself were equal to the best in the land and which he sent up to Chicago with confident expectation of getting "the top of the market," should sell fifty cents per 100 lbs. below the price obtained the same day by his neighbor who had what he derisively called "high fangled notions" on the subject of blooded stock. It had taken the farmer three years and more to make his cattle worth $5.50. while his wide-awake neighbor who, by observation and experience, had learned the value of good blood, had in a year's less time and by the expenditure of one-third less in food produced animals worth fifty cents per 100 lbs. more in any market in the land. Examples of this kind by the score may be seen any day at the Chicago stock yards. And the difference is as marked in horses and hogs and sheep as in cattle.--[Breeders Gazette.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Breeders Gazette on the market premium for blooded stock.

articles.text: The arrivals of cattle on the Chicago market averaged about 6,000 a day during the last week and up to Monday night, against about 7,000 daily for the previous week. Through Texans sold at $2,25 @ 2,80 for cows and $2,60 @ 3,40 for steers. Western range cattle sold at $2,75 @ 5, with few rates over $4, and many as low as $3. Wintered Texans sold as high as $3,75. articles.headline: Cowboys in the West.
articles.text: We are glad to record that our eastern and northern publications are forming a more correct conception, and giving to their readers a truer portrait of the Texas and western cowboy. The National Stockman of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, says: "The typical ranchman is no swaggering desperado or animated arsenal; but is a business man and gentleman. If the national political convention to be held in Chicago in the next few months shows a better average of citizenship than was exhibited recently at Cheyenne, W. T., when four hundred and fifty ranchmen met in convention to deliberate on matters affecting their interests, they will reflect the highest credit on the nation they represent. A few years hence the standard of personal character and public demeanor will be as high on the plains of the trans-Missouri country as it now is in Pennsylvania. The ranch hands now employed for the work once performed wholly by the knights of the derringer are of a character which must in a few years rob the life of the herder of much of its risk and the blood-and-thunder press of most of its atrocious sensations. A great many farmers' sons, raised to habits of industry and trained in the usages of good society, are filling up vacancies which occur among herdsmen, and in many places they preponderate among the employes of the district. They take this method of learning the business from the very beginning, and are effecting a revolution in it as thorough as it is gratifying. We are personally acquainted with young men of character, intelligence, education, and even of moderate wealth, who are now, with the end referred to in view, voluntarily undertaking the hardships of the herder's lot. And we are in correspondence with others, of equal personal worth, whose applications are already filed, and who are only awaiting an opportuity to change the farm for the ranch. There can be but one outcome to all this, an outcome to which the whole country, and especially the west, must look forward to with satisfaction." Formerly he was unjustly classed as "wild and wooly," a dare devil, and outlaw. This character was given to the class simply because a few desperadoes occasionally were found in the ranks. They were the thieves and outlaws who were among, but not really of the cowboys. They gave the unsavory reputation to the ranches, and when stock associations were organized and the ranch business systematized this class were hounded out. Now there are no truer, better or more deserving men in the west than can be found among the managers and employes of cattle ranches.
articles.summary: Commentary, quoting the National Stockman, defending the character of the western cowboy and ranchman.

articles.headline: The Mustang.
articles.text:
The wild horse of America, although now native to the soil, is descended from the tribes of wild horses that still rove the plains of Central Asia. When the discoverers of this continent first landed, there were no horses anywhere in either North or South America. Centuries before, the horse had been introduced into European countries from Asia, and had become common all over that continent. When Columbus arrived here on his second voyage, in 1493, he was accompanied by one Cabæa de Vaca, who brought with him a number of horses, which were landed in Florida.

Cortez took horses with him to assist in the conquest of Mexico, as did Pizarro in his conquest of Peru. The natives were greatly affrighted when they beheld these strange animals. At first they supposed that the man and the horse were one complete creature, something like the centaur of which we read in ancient fable. And when they saw the rider dismount and disengage himself from his steed, their amazement knew no bounds.

In time, the savages learned that the horse was an animal that had been subdued by man, and that it was a separate creature; but they long dreaded the horse of the Spaniards as a beast of prey. And when the horses escaped from their masters and made their way into the forest, as they did after a space, the natives avoided them as something to be shunned. The quarreling Spaniards neglected their steeds, which soon found homes on the plains of Mexico, South America, and the unexplored regions of North America. From these escaped animals have sprung the wild horses of America. The mustang, as the native horse of the North American continent is usually called, is generally of a bright chestnut color. The horses marked with odd colors and patches are called "pinto" or "painted," by the Mexicans and "calico" by the Americans. The mustang is smaller than the domesticated American horse; for we must remember that the larger horses now found in our stables are the direct descendents of later importations from Europe.--[St. Nicholas.
articles.summary: Reprint from St. Nicholas on the origin of the American mustang.

articles.text: Saturday and Monday were consumed by the court at Bismarck in obtaining a jury in the Marquis' case, resulting in the following being chosen: "W. S. Moorhouse, Frank Frisby, C. H. Edick, F. W. McKinney, C. R. Williams, Timothy Griffin, F. E. Young, C. W. Renard, George Wahl, Anson Northrup, W. B. Watson and B. F. Gage. The prosecution will try to prove that Wannegan, Luffsey and O'Donald were riding home when they were fired at by concealed parties. That twenty-five or thirty shots were fired. That Luffsey was then killed. That Marquis de Mores fired the fatal shot. That there was a feud between O'Donald and Paddock. That Paddock falsely represented to De Mores that his life was in danger and instigated him to join this attempt to put O'Donald out of the way. The first witness when the case was called Tuesday morning was James McShane. He testified that he was working on the railroad about two hundred yards from the scene of the shooting. That he saw the Marquis and others come out of the brush with guns in their hands. That he went to where Luffsey's body lay and also to the thicket where he found the brush cut away and tramped down. Paul Heinze exhibited a sketch of the scene, showing the relative positions of the parties. McNeave Nally testified that he was on the coroner's jury and described the wound which caused Luffsey's death.
articles.summary: Report of jury selection and the opening prosecution testimony in the Marquis de Morès murder trial at Bismarck.

events.title: Prosecution rests in the de Morès murder trial
events.summary: A special dispatch from Bismarck reported the prosecution had rested, having proved only that Luffsey was killed by a party that included de Morès.
events.excerpt: The prosecution rested yesterday, having only proved what is already known, that Luffsey was killed by the party, of which DeMores was a member.

events.date_basis: "This morning" in dispatch dated Sept. 17 (Thu 17 Sep 1885)
events.title: Witnesses testify Luffsey and O'Donald threatened to shoot de Morès
events.summary: Witnesses McClung, Harmon and Walker testified they heard Luffsey and O'Donald say they would shoot de Morès on sight; other testimony went to the pair's bad reputations.
events.excerpt: heard Luffsey and O'Donald say the day before the shooting that they would shoot DeMores on sight.

events.date_basis: "This morning" in dispatch dated Sept. 17 (Thu 17 Sep 1885)
events.title: Judge Francis jails prosecutor T. K. Long for contempt
events.summary: During the de Morès trial, prosecuting attorney T. K. Long quarreled with Judge Francis and gave him the lie direct; the judge committed Long to jail for contempt.
events.excerpt: The Judge immediately committed Long to jail for contempt of court, where he now languishes.

events.title: Jury chosen for the Marquis de Morès trial at Bismarck
events.summary: The court at Bismarck spent Saturday and Monday seating the jury in the Marquis' case; twelve jurors were named.
events.excerpt: Saturday and Monday were consumed by the court at Bismarck in obtaining a jury in the Marquis' case

events.title: Opening testimony in de Morès trial: James McShane and coroner's juror
events.summary: The prosecution outlined its case that de Morès fired the fatal shot at Luffsey, with Paddock instigating him; railroad worker James McShane testified he saw the Marquis and others come out of the brush with guns, Paul Heinze exhibited a sketch, and McNeave Nally described the wound.
events.excerpt: That he saw the Marquis and others come out of the brush with guns in their hands.

events.date_basis: witnesses subpoenaed days ahead; "last Saturday" (12 Sep) before Thu 17 Sep 1885
events.title: Medora empties as witnesses go to Bismarck for de Morès trial
events.summary: The Cow Boy said so many residents were subpoenaed to the Marquis' trial that Medora's streets looked deserted, and mocked Bismarck for profiting from witnesses who were 'decently broke' by last Saturday.
events.excerpt: Our streets look deserted, owing to the number of witnesses subpœnæd from here on Marquis' trial.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before issue
events.title: Sioux Falls convention settles on 'Dacotah' and compulsory schooling
events.summary: The paper reported the Sioux Falls constitutional convention had about decided on the state name "Dacotah," the motto "Under God the people rule" and compulsory school attendance from six to twelve.
events.excerpt: the name of the new state shall be "Dacotah" with a "c" and a "haich,"

events.date_basis: no date given; week before issue
events.title: Cow Boy urges organization of Billings County
events.summary: The paper argued Billings County should organize immediately under the new territorial law, with commissioners recommended by petition, and advised paying any Stark County taxes under protest.
events.excerpt: we advise that any taxes paid to Stark county be paid under protest

events.title: Magill case ends in manslaughter verdict
events.summary: The jury in the Magill case returned a verdict of manslaughter in the second degree; sentence was expected in a day or two.
events.excerpt: The verdict in this, the Magill case, was "Manslaughter in the second degree."

events.title: Fall round-up to begin September 29
events.summary: The paper announced the fall round-up would begin on the 29th.
events.excerpt: Fall round-up begins the 29th.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before issue
events.title: Mrs. Arch. Boyd ill
events.summary: Mrs. Arch. Boyd, wife of the Northern Pacific Hotel's proprietor, had been ill with severe tooth pain and was recovering.
events.excerpt: suffering severe pain from her teeth. She is now recovering.

events.title: J. H. Ellison returns from Mandan
events.summary: J. H. Ellison returned from several days' visit in Mandan.
events.excerpt: J. H. Ellison returned from Mandan Tuesday evening

events.title: Mingusville district beef round-up begins
events.summary: The beef round-up for the Mingusville district started from the mouth of Glendive creek, with R. H. Moore as foreman.
events.excerpt: The beef round-up for the Mingusville district started the 15th., from the mouth of Glendive creek.

events.title: Mr. and Mrs. McKee leave for Pittsburgh
events.summary: Mr. and Mrs. McKee left for home in Pittsburgh after a long visit, planning to return.
events.excerpt: They have had a long and enjoyable visit here and propose to repeat the trip.

events.title: T. W. Ingersoll departs after hunting and photographing
events.summary: T. W. Ingersoll left for St. Paul after a ten-day stay in which he hunted and took many photographic views.
events.excerpt: he took not only a hunt, but a large number of photographic views

events.title: J. C. Fisher back from Wadsworth's beef round-up
events.summary: J. C. Fisher returned from Wadsworth's beef round-up.
events.excerpt: what he don't know about being a cowboy--would fill a large book.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before issue
events.title: Range burned from Andrews to Sentinel Butte
events.summary: Fires along the railroad nearly destroyed the range from about three miles beyond Andrews to near Sentinel Butte and north to Knutson creek.
events.excerpt: the range is nearly destroyed by fire.

events.title: Bad Lands Cattle Co. finishes round-up, drives 309 head to Dickinson
events.summary: The Bad Lands Cattle Co. finished its round-up and started 309 head, averaging nearly 1400 pounds, for shipment from Dickinson, probably on Saturday.
events.excerpt: the best lot of cattle that have been shipped east from Dakota or Montana this year.

events.title: Henry Boice in Medora
events.summary: Henry Boice was in town Monday.
events.excerpt: Henry Boice was in town Monday.

events.title: Another Medora wedding expected
events.summary: The paper hinted that another wedding was coming soon.
events.excerpt: Another wedding is an event of the near future.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before issue
events.title: J. W. Foley of Bismarck visits on Refrigerator Car Co. business
events.summary: J. W. Foley of Bismarck was in Medora on business of the Refrigerator Car Co.
events.excerpt: is here on business of the Ref. Car Co.

events.title: Delivery of 500 Hashknife cattle at Medora
events.summary: John W. Buster superintended the delivery of five hundred Hashknife cattle averaging about 1080 pounds.
events.excerpt: superintended the delivery of five hundred Hashknife cattle, averaging about 1080 pounds.

events.title: Ranchers rebuild Davis creek bridge
events.summary: Ranches up the river jointly replaced the Davis creek bridge near the Custer Trail ranch, which the last storm had washed out.
events.excerpt: The ranches up the river chipped in last Monday and replaced the Davis creek bridge near the Custer trail ranch.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before issue
events.title: Dr. Jorgens enlarges his drug store
events.summary: Dr. Jorgens was building a dwelling addition to his drug store; his family planned a trip to the Cave Hills before wintering in Medora.
events.excerpt: Dr. Jorgens is building an addition to his drug store for dwelling purposes.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before issue
events.title: Medora packing company put on short time
events.summary: Low cattle and beef prices in Chicago forced 'the Co. here' to work short time.
events.excerpt: has forced the Co. here to work on short time.

events.title: Chas. Cook closing out store before leaving Medora
events.summary: Chas. Cook advertised a sale of his entire stock at cost, and his fixtures, before his removal from Medora.
events.excerpt: Previous to my removal from Medora, I will sell all goods in my store

events.title: Sheriff's sale of Little Missouri Land and Stock Co. property
events.summary: Morton County's sheriff gave notice he would auction horses, wagons, machinery and furniture of the Little Missouri Land and Stock Company at the Cantonment near Medora on September 28 to satisfy a roughly $390 judgment for James and Ira C. Bellows.
events.excerpt: will sell at Public Auction at the Cantonment, about one mile west of the town of Medora

events.title: A. T. Packard offers cattle for sale
events.summary: Packard advertised a small herd of Minnesota and Iowa cattle, with horses and outfit, for sale.
events.excerpt: Six cows, twelve two-year-old steers, ninety two and three-year-old heifers

events.title: Howard Eaton's bay gelding strays
events.summary: Howard Eaton advertised for a four-year-old bay gelding lost about April 15.
events.excerpt: About April 15, a bay gelding four years old, branded pickaxe s, on left shoulder

events.title: J. A. Van Eeghen offers reward for strayed horse
events.summary: J. A. Van Eeghen offered $10 for return of a buckskin horse branded circle bar.
events.excerpt: One buckskin horse, branded circle bar on right hip and right shoulder.

events.title: Chimney Butte Ranch brand ad lists Theodore Roosevelt as proprietor
events.summary: The paper's standing brand advertisement listed the Chimney Butte Ranch with Theodore Roosevelt as proprietor and Ferris & Merrifield as managers, ranging six miles south of the railroad on the Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: CHIMNEY BUTTE RANCH. THEODORE ROOSEVELT, Proprietor. FERRIS & MERRIFIELD, Managers.

events.title: E. G. Paddock brand ad
events.summary: E. G. Paddock, co-defendant in the de Morès case, carried a brand advertisement for his circle-dot cattle and horses north of the N. P. crossing.
events.excerpt: E. G. PADDOCK, Postoffice Address, MEDORA, DAK.
